newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ABB says no plans to cut nuclear links.
newsitem.headline: ABB says no plans to cut nuclear links.

text.p: ABB Sweden, the Swedish operations of Swiss-Swedish electrical engineer Asea Brown Boveri (ABB), said on Friday it had no plans to reduce its operations dependent on the nuclear power industry despite a government agreement to phase out nuclear power.
"We will continue to invest in nuclear power. There is a big nuclear power capacity in Sweden that I assume will remain," Anders Narvinger, managing director of ABB Sweden told Reuters.

Sweden's minority Social Democrats government and Left and Centre parties finalised an energy agreement this year under which one of Sweden 12 nuclear reactors would be closed in 1998 and a second in 2001.
Further details about the phase out would be settled later.
Narvinger said the agreement meant that electricity intensive industries in Sweden would be faced with a more competitive marketplace with accompanying lower investment.
Power intensive industries account for about five billion crowns ($666.4 million) of ABB Sweden's total yearly income.
The company's sales to the nuclear industry in Sweden account for about one billion crowns a year with about 200 million crowns of this coming from Barseback, whose two reactors will be closed.
The ABB group's target is to show a volume growth of about six percent a year over the economic cycle.
The business cycle in Western Europe was not expected to turn up before 1998 so 1997 was seen to be a bit of a middle year.
West Europe, excluding Sweden, accounted for 27 percent of ABB's income in 1996.
Narvinger estimated that growing markets in Asia, Eastern Europe and Latin America will increase the company's income.
He also said that exports would make up a big part of the company's future sales.
ABB on Thursday posted a lower-than-expected profit for 1996 showing a six percent fall in group net income to $1.23 billion from $1.32 billion in 1995.
The company said it expected 1997 net income to reach at least the same level as in 1996.
-- Kristina Zetterlund, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1005 ($ = 7.503 Swedish Crowns)
